docs.title: Wally
docs.text:
Wally is a Java library that lets a program write down events very quickly, never lose them, and hand them to other parts of the program in order.

New here?

You don't need to be a Java expert to follow these docs. Words that might be new are linked to the Glossary. For the Java side of things, read How Wally works.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Imagine an online shop on a busy sale day. Thousands of orders arrive every second. The shop has two needs:

  1. Never lose an order. If the server crashes, every order it already said "OK" to must still be there when it restarts.
  2. Hand orders to workers fast. Different parts of the system (payment, shipping, email) each need to see every order, in the order it arrived, without slowing each other down.

The usual Java tools for passing messages between parts of a program (called queues) work, but at very high speeds they hit two problems:

  • Waiting in line. Only one thread can use the queue at a time, so the others wait. This is called lock contention.
  • Cleanup pauses. Every message creates a new Java object. Java periodically pauses the program to clean up old objects (garbage collection). Those pauses can be milliseconds long, which is a lifetime for a system handling millions of events.

Wally is built to avoid both.

docs.title: What Wally does
docs.text:
Wally does two jobs with one data structure.

Job 1: a logbook (Write-Ahead Log)Job 2: an order rail (Event Queue)

Think of a ship's logbook written in pen. Every event is written on the next free line, in order, and never erased or changed. If something goes wrong, you can read the logbook from the start and know exactly what happened.

Databases use this trick: before changing anything, they write what they are about to do into a log. After a crash, they replay the log. This is a Write-Ahead Log (WAL).

Think of a restaurant kitchen. Waiters pin order tickets on a rail, left to right. Each cook reads the tickets in order and keeps a bookmark showing how far they've got. The grill cook and the dessert cook read the same tickets, at their own pace.

In Wally, waiters are producers, cooks are consumers, and bookmarks are cursors. That makes Wally an event queue.

Because both jobs are "write events in order, read them in order", Wally uses one log for both. The only difference is when old pages get thrown away.

flowchart LR
    P1[Producer: web server] -->|append| L
    P2[Producer: mobile API] -->|append| L
    subgraph L[Wally log]
        direction LR
        S1[segment 0] --> S2[segment 1] --> S3[segment 2 ...]
    end
    L -->|read at own pace| C1[Consumer: payments]
    L -->|read at own pace| C2[Consumer: shipping]

docs.title: How Wally does it
docs.text:
Five ideas, in plain language. How Wally works explains each one with the actual Java code.

1. One long notebook, split into pages. Events are appended one after another into fixed-size files called segments. When a page fills up, Wally starts the next one. Every event gets a position: its distance in bytes from the very start of the log, like a page-and-line number.

2. Write straight into a file's memory. Wally uses memory-mapped files. The operating system makes a file look like a block of memory, so writing to that memory is writing to the file. There is no separate "save" step for every event, and the operating system writes it to disk in the background.

3. Work outside Java's cleanup zone. Normal Java objects live on the heap, which the garbage collector manages. Wally keeps events off-heap in raw memory and reuses the few objects it needs. No new objects per event means nothing for the garbage collector to clean, so there are no cleanup pauses. This is what zero-allocation means.

4. No waiting in line. Instead of a lock, producers take a ticket, like at a deli counter. One tiny atomic instruction hands each producer its own slot in the log, and they all write at the same time without blocking each other. This is called lock-free.

5. Write the record, then sign it. A reader must never see a half-written event. So a producer writes the event first and writes its length last, like signing a form only after filling it in. A reader that sees a length of zero knows "not finished yet, wait here." Java's memory ordering rules guarantee that once the length is visible, the whole event is too.

docs.title: What using it will look like
docs.text:
Coming in milestone M1

The public API below is being built. Today, the lower-level building blocks exist and are tested. See the Roadmap.

try (Wally wal = Wally.builder().dir(Path.of("data/orders")).open()) {

    // Producer side: write an event
    Appender appender = wal.appender();
    appender.append(orderBytes, 0, orderBytes.length);

    // Consumer side: read events in order, at your own pace
    Tailer payments = wal.tailer("payments");
    payments.poll((buffer, offset, length, position) -> {
        // handle one order here
    }, 100);
}

Status

Pre-alpha. Milestone M0 (off-heap memory layer and single-segment log) is done. See the Roadmap.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
• Harness: JMH for throughput; a fixed-rate driver + HdrHistogram for latency (from M2), to avoid coordinated omission.
  • Scenarios: 1P1C and NP1C (N = 1, 2, 4, 8); payloads 32 B, 256 B, 4 KB; flush policies none, periodic(1ms/5ms), sync.
  • Baselines: ArrayBlockingQueue, JCTools MPSC, LMAX Disruptor, Chronicle Queue.
  • Allocation: JMH -prof gc (gc.alloc.rate.norm) and an Epsilon GC run.
  • Environment: record CPU, kernel, JDK, JVM flags, core pinning. Publish raw data and the script that produced it.

docs.title: Reproduce
docs.text: ./gradlew :wally-bench:jmh -Pjmh.profilers=gc

docs.title: M0: single-thread append + read
docs.text:
SegmentLogBenchmark: one thread appends a record and reads it back. Measures the raw cost of framing, the release/acquire publish and the copy, plus allocation.

Environment: Apple M4 Pro, macOS 26.4.1, Temurin 25.0.5, JMH 1.37, 1 fork, 3×1 s warmup, 5×1 s measurement, laptop (no core pinning).

Benchmark 32 B 256 B 4 KB Allocation wallyClaimCommitRead (zero copy) 5.95 ns 8.52 ns 42.3 ns ≈ 0 B/op wallyAppendRead (copy in) 7.79 ns 12.5 ns 103 ns ≈ 0 B/op arrayBlockingQueueOfferPoll (new byte[] per message) 10.1 ns 11.6 ns 91.2 ns payload + 16 B/op

How to read these numbers

  • Single-threaded, so there is no lock contention. ArrayBlockingQueue's real cost appears under contention and as GC pressure over time. Those effects show up in the cross-thread benchmarks (M2).
  • The 1 MB benchmark buffer is re-zeroed when full. At 4 KB that happens every ~255 records and inflates the Wally numbers. In the real log, new segments are zeroed ahead of time by the preallocator (M1).
  • Laptop numbers. Reference results will come from dedicated Linux hardware.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
Draft

Filled in as milestones land.

Term Meaning Log Append-only sequence of records spread across fixed-size segment files. Position 64-bit logical byte address of a record: segmentIndex * segmentSize + offset. Monotonic, never reused. Segment One pre-sized, memory-mapped file (%020d.wly). Starts with a 64 B header. Record 16 B header + payload, 8 B aligned. length == 0 means not yet committed. Claim / commit Two-phase write: reserve space, write the payload in place, publish by writing length with release semantics. Appender Per-thread write handle. Reuses one Claim flyweight. Tailer Read handle. Polls records via a callback (segment, offset, length, position). Consumer group Named tailer whose position is persisted in the cursor file. Flush policy When page-cache data is forced to disk: none, periodic, sync. Flushed position Highest position guaranteed durable under the current flush policy. Checkpoint WAL-mode marker: everything below it may be deleted. Retention Deletes segments wholly below the minimum of all group cursors and the checkpoint.

docs.title: File format
docs.text:
Draft

Finalized in M1. All integers are little-endian. Format version: 1.

docs.title: Segment file
docs.text: Name: %020d.wly (segment index, zero-padded). Size: fixed segmentSize (power of two).

docs.title: Segment header (64 B)
docs.text: Offset Size Field 0 6 magic WALLY\0 6 2 format version 8 8 segment size 16 8 base position (segmentIndex * segmentSize) 24 36 reserved (zero) 60 4 CRC32C of bytes 0–59

docs.title: Record (starts at a multiple of 8)
docs.text:
Offset Size Field 0 4 frameLength: header + payload bytes (unaligned); 0 = uncommitted. Written last, with release semantics. 4 2 type: 1 = DATA, 2 = PADDING 6 2 flags 8 4 CRC32C of the payload (0 when ChecksumMode.NONE) 12 4 reserved 16 frameLength - 16 payload — 0–7 alignment padding to the next multiple of 8

A PADDING frame fills the remainder of a segment when the next record doesn't fit, and replaces aborted claims. It only uses frameLength and type, so it can be as short as 8 bytes. Because frames and segment ends are 8-aligned, the gap to fill is never smaller than that.

Why the frame length includes the header

A payload-length field would make a header-only padding frame encode as 0, which already means "uncommitted".

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Each entry has two parts:

  • In general: what the word means in everyday software engineering.
  • In Wally: what it means in this project specifically.

Terms are in alphabetical order. Words in italics inside an entry have their own entry.

docs.title: Acquire / release
docs.text:
In general: Rules about the order in which one thread sees another thread's writes to memory. Modern CPUs and compilers reorder instructions to go faster, so without rules thread B might see thread A's second write before its first. A release write means "everything I wrote before this is visible to anyone who sees this write." An acquire read means "once I've seen this value, I'll also see everything written before it."

In Wally: The producer fills in a record, then writes its length with a release write. The reader reads the length with an acquire read. If the reader sees a non-zero length, it's guaranteed to see the complete record. See Mem.setIntRelease and Mem.getIntAcquire.

docs.title: Alignment
docs.text:
In general: Placing data at memory addresses that are multiples of some number (2, 4, 8...). CPUs read aligned data faster, and some atomic instructions only work on aligned data.

In Wally: Every record starts at a multiple of 8 bytes. If a record is 19 bytes, the next one starts 24 bytes later. The extra bytes are wasted on purpose.

docs.title: Allocation
docs.text:
In general: Asking for memory to hold something. In Java, new Something() allocates an object on the heap. Allocation itself is cheap, but every allocated object eventually has to be cleaned up by garbage collection.

In Wally: The goal is no allocation per event. See zero-allocation.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
In general: Application Programming Interface: the set of classes and methods a library offers to the people who use it. It's the library's "front door".

In Wally: Everything in the io.wally.api package, such as Claim and RecordHandler. Everything else is internal and can change without notice.

docs.title: Appender
docs.text:
In general: Something that adds items to the end of a sequence.

In Wally: The object a producer uses to write records. Each thread gets its own appender, which reuses one claim object for every record.

docs.title: Append-only
docs.text:
In general: Data that is only ever added at the end, never changed or deleted in the middle. Simple, fast, and easy to recover after a crash.

In Wally: The log is append-only. Old data is removed only by deleting whole segments (see retention).

docs.title: Arena
docs.text:
In general: A memory-management pattern where many allocations share one lifetime and are freed together.

In Wally: Java's java.lang.foreign.Arena. Off-heap memory and mapped files are tied to an arena, and closing the arena frees or unmaps them all at once, at a moment Wally chooses.

docs.title: Atomic operation
docs.text:
In general: An operation that happens all at once from the point of view of other threads: nobody can see it half-done. Examples: "add 5 to this number and give me the old value" (fetch-and-add), or "set this to X only if it's still Y" (CAS).

In Wally: Producers use one atomic fetch-and-add on the log's tail to reserve space, so two producers never get the same slot. See lock-free.

docs.title: Backpressure
docs.text:
In general: When a system slows down or refuses new work because the next stage can't keep up, instead of running out of memory or crashing.

In Wally: In queue mode, if the slowest consumer falls too far behind, appending returns a BACK_PRESSURED code instead of growing the log forever.

docs.title: Benchmark
docs.text:
In general: A program that measures how fast something is, in a repeatable way.

In Wally: The wally-bench module uses JMH to measure how many nanoseconds an append and read take and how many bytes they allocate. See Benchmarks.

docs.title: Byte / byte order (endianness)
docs.text:
In general: A byte is 8 bits, the basic unit of memory. A number bigger than one byte (an int is 4 bytes) can be stored lowest byte first (little-endian) or highest byte first (big-endian).

In Wally: All numbers in Wally's files are little-endian, which matches the CPUs Wally supports (x86-64 and ARM64).

docs.title: Cache line
docs.text:
In general: CPUs don't read memory one byte at a time. They read it in chunks called cache lines (usually 64 bytes) and keep copies in fast caches close to each core.

In Wally: Counters written by different threads are kept far apart in memory so they don't share a cache line. See false sharing.

docs.title: CAS (compare-and-swap)
docs.text:
In general: An atomic operation: "if the value is still X, change it to Y, and tell me whether it worked." The building block of most lock-free code. If another thread changed it first, you retry.

In Wally: Used where retrying is fine (for example, updating cursors). For the hot path of claiming space, Wally uses fetch-and-add, which never needs a retry. See ADR 0004.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
In general: A point in a log that says "everything before here has been safely processed elsewhere."

In Wally: In WAL mode, the application calls checkpoint(position) to tell Wally that segments before that position may be deleted.

docs.title: Checksum (CRC32C)
docs.text:
In general: A small number calculated from a block of data. If even one bit of the data changes, the checksum almost certainly changes too, so you can detect corruption. CRC32C is a common, fast checksum.

In Wally: Each record can store a CRC32C of its payload. After a crash, recovery uses it to detect records that were only half written to disk.

docs.title: Claim
docs.text:
In general: Reserving something before using it.

In Wally: Reserving space in the log for a record, then writing the data directly into that space (zero-copy), then committing. The Claim interface represents this reserved space.

docs.title: Commit
docs.text:
In general: Making a change final and visible.

In Wally: Writing a record's length with a release write (see acquire / release). Until then, readers treat the record as not existing yet.

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text:
In general: Several things in progress at the same time, usually on different threads. Hard to get right because threads can interfere with each other in surprising ways.

In Wally: Many producers can append at once, and readers read while producers write, all without locks.

docs.title: Consumer
docs.text:
In general: The part of a system that receives and processes messages.

In Wally: Code that reads records from the log through a tailer.

docs.title: Consumer group
docs.text:
In general: A named reader that remembers where it got to, so it can continue after a restart. (Kafka popularized the term.)

In Wally: A tailer with a name, like "payments". Its cursor is saved to disk.

docs.title: Crash recovery
docs.text:
In general: What a system does when it starts after an unexpected stop, to get back to a correct state.

In Wally: On startup, Wally reads the log from the last checkpoint, checks each record's checksum, and cuts the log off at the first record that is incomplete or corrupt.

docs.title: Cursor
docs.text:
In general: A marker that remembers a position, like a bookmark.

In Wally: A position in the log that a consumer group has read up to.

docs.title: Durability
docs.text:
In general: The promise that once the system says "saved", the data survives a crash or power failure.

In Wally: Controlled by the flush policy. See Guarantees.

docs.title: Epsilon GC
docs.text:
In general: A special Java garbage collector that never collects anything. When memory runs out, the program crashes. It's used for testing and for very short-lived programs.

In Wally: Used as a test: Wally appends and reads 50 million records with Epsilon GC and a small heap. If Wally allocated even one byte per record, the program would run out of memory and fail.

docs.title: Event
docs.text:
In general: A record that something happened, like "order #123 placed".

In Wally: Used interchangeably with record: a chunk of bytes appended to the log.

docs.title: Event queue
docs.text:
In general: A queue of events, where producers add events and consumers process them.

In Wally: One of Wally's two modes: the log plus named cursors plus retention.

docs.title: False sharing
docs.text:
In general: A performance problem where two threads write to different variables that happen to sit on the same cache line. The CPU cores keep stealing the line from each other, so both slow down as if they were sharing the same variable.

In Wally: Hot counters, such as the log's tail, are surrounded by 128 bytes of empty padding to avoid this.

docs.title: FFM API (Foreign Function & Memory API)
docs.text:
In general: A modern Java API (final since Java 22) for working with memory outside the heap and calling native code, safely and quickly.

In Wally: The foundation of Wally: MemorySegment, Arena, ValueLayout and VarHandle all come from it. It replaces the old, unsupported sun.misc.Unsafe. See ADR 0001.

docs.title: Flush / fsync
docs.text:
In general: Forcing data that the operating system is holding in memory (the page cache) to be written to the physical disk.

In Wally: Done with MemorySegment.force(). When and how often depends on the flush policy.

docs.title: Flush policy
docs.text:
In general: A rule for how often to flush. Flushing more often is safer but slower.

In Wally: none() (let the OS decide), periodic(5ms) (every few milliseconds, many records at once) or sync() (before every append returns).

docs.title: Flyweight
docs.text:
In general: A design pattern where one small object is reused to look at many pieces of data, instead of creating one object per piece.

In Wally: The Claim object is reused for every record an appender writes, so no object is created per record.

docs.title: Frame / record
docs.text:
In general: A chunk of data with a small header describing it (length, type...).

In Wally: A 16-byte header plus the payload. The header holds the frame length, the type (DATA or PADDING), flags and a checksum. See File format.

docs.title: Garbage collection (GC)
docs.text:
In general: Java's automatic memory cleanup. You create objects; when nothing refers to them anymore, the garbage collector frees their memory. It's convenient, but the collector sometimes has to pause your program, and the more objects you create, the more work it has.

In Wally: The thing Wally is designed to avoid on its fast path. It keeps data off-heap and creates no objects per record.

docs.title: Gradle
docs.text:
In general: A build tool for Java. It downloads libraries, compiles code, runs tests and packages the result.

In Wally: Configured by the *.gradle.kts files. Run ./gradlew check to build and test everything.

docs.title: Heap
docs.text:
In general: The memory area where Java stores objects created with new. It's managed by the garbage collector.

In Wally: Wally keeps record data off-heap so the garbage collector never has to look at it.

docs.title: Hot path
docs.text:
In general: The code that runs most often, like for every single message. This is where performance matters most.

In Wally: Appending, claiming, committing and reading records.

docs.title: JIT compiler
docs.text:
In general: Java first runs your code slowly, interpreted, then the Just-In-Time compiler turns frequently used code into fast machine code while the program runs.

In Wally: Tests and benchmarks "warm up" first, so they measure the fast compiled code rather than the slow start.

docs.title: JMH
docs.text:
In general: Java Microbenchmark Harness, the standard tool for measuring small pieces of Java code accurately. It handles warm-up, repetition and statistics for you.

In Wally: Used in wally-bench. Its gc profiler shows how many bytes each operation allocates.

docs.title: JPMS (Java modules)
docs.text:
In general: The Java Platform Module System. A module-info.java file declares which packages other code may use.

In Wally: wally-core exports only io.wally.api, so users can't accidentally depend on internal code.

docs.title: JVM
docs.text:
In general: The Java Virtual Machine, the program that runs compiled Java code.

In Wally: Wally needs a JVM for Java 25 or newer.

docs.title: Latency
docs.text:
In general: How long one operation takes, such as from "send" to "received". Often reported as percentiles: p99 = 99% of operations were faster than this. The rare slow ones are called tail latency.

In Wally: Measured in nanoseconds. Avoiding GC pauses mainly improves tail latency.

docs.title: Lock
docs.text:
In general: A mechanism that lets only one thread into a piece of code at a time. Safe and simple, but other threads must wait (contention), and a thread holding a lock can be paused by the OS while everyone waits for it.

In Wally: Not used on the hot path.

docs.title: Lock-free
docs.text:
In general: Code where threads coordinate with atomic operations instead of locks, so a paused thread never stops the others from making progress.

In Wally: Appending and reading are lock-free. Flushing to disk is not, since the operating system itself may block.

docs.title: Memory-mapped file
docs.text:
In general: The operating system makes a file appear as a block of memory. Reading or writing that memory reads or writes the file, and the OS moves data between memory and disk in the background.

In Wally: Every segment file is memory-mapped. Appending a record is just writing to memory, with no per-record system call.

docs.title: MemorySegment
docs.text:
In general: Java's (FFM API) safe handle to a block of memory, either on-heap, off-heap or a memory-mapped file. It knows its size, so out-of-bounds access throws an error instead of corrupting memory.

In Wally: All record data is read and written through MemorySegments.

docs.title: Off-heap
docs.text:
In general: Memory outside the Java heap, which the garbage collector doesn't manage. You decide when it's freed.

In Wally: Where all records live.

docs.title: Padding
docs.text:
In general: Empty space added on purpose, for alignment, to avoid false sharing, or to fill a gap.

In Wally: (1) Bytes added after a record to reach an 8-byte boundary. (2) A PADDING frame that fills the end of a segment when the next record doesn't fit, or replaces an aborted claim. Readers skip padding frames.

docs.title: Page cache
docs.text:
In general: Memory the operating system uses to hold recently used file data. Writes go here first and reach the disk later.

In Wally: Writes to a memory-mapped segment land in the page cache. They survive Wally crashing, but not the whole machine losing power, unless flushed.

docs.title: Page fault
docs.text:
In general: When a program touches memory the OS hasn't loaded yet, the OS pauses the program briefly to load or create that page. Usually invisible, but expensive on a hot path.

In Wally: A background task prepares the next segment before it's needed, so producers don't hit page faults when switching segments.

docs.title: Payload
docs.text:
In general: The actual data being carried, as opposed to headers about it.

In Wally: The bytes the user appends. Wally doesn't care what's inside them.

docs.title: Position
docs.text:
In general: Where something is in a sequence.

In Wally: A record's distance in bytes from the very start of the log, across all segments: segmentIndex × segmentSize + offsetInSegment. Positions only ever grow. See ADR 0002.

docs.title: Producer
docs.text:
In general: The part of a system that creates and sends messages.

In Wally: Code that appends records through an appender.

docs.title: Queue
docs.text:
In general: A first-in, first-out (FIFO) line: items come out in the order they went in. Java has many built in, such as ArrayBlockingQueue.

In Wally: Wally behaves like a queue, but records are kept in files, every consumer gets every record, and nothing is removed when it's read.

docs.title: Race condition
docs.text:
In general: A bug where the result depends on the exact timing of threads. These are notoriously hard to reproduce because they only show up sometimes.

In Wally: Prevented by the claim/commit protocol and acquire / release ordering. Tools like jcstress (see the table at the end) test for them.

docs.title: Retention
docs.text:
In general: How long data is kept before it's deleted.

In Wally: A segment is deleted only once every consumer group has read past it and, in WAL mode, it's before the last checkpoint.

docs.title: Segment
docs.text:
In general: One piece of something split into pieces.

In Wally: One fixed-size, memory-mapped file of the log, such as 00000000000000000003.wly. Deleting old data means deleting whole segment files.

docs.title: Serialization
docs.text:
In general: Turning an object into bytes (to save or send it) and back again (deserialization).

In Wally: Wally stores bytes and doesn't care how you serialize. Zero-copy formats like SBE fit best, because you can write fields straight into the claimed space.

docs.title: Single writer principle
docs.text:
In general: A performance rule: if only one thread ever writes a piece of data, you need no locks or atomic operations for it.

In Wally: Single-producer mode is the default and fastest. Multi-producer mode is opt-in.

docs.title: Tailer
docs.text:
In general: A reader that follows the end of a log as it grows, like the tail -f command.

In Wally: The object you read records with. It calls your RecordHandler for each record.

docs.title: Thread
docs.text:
In general: An independent path of execution inside a program. Several threads can run at once on different CPU cores, sharing the same memory.

In Wally: Producers and consumers typically run on different threads.

docs.title: Throughput
docs.text:
In general: How many operations happen per second.

In Wally: Millions of records per second per producer. See Benchmarks.

docs.title: Torn write
docs.text:
In general: A write that was only partly saved when a crash happened, so half the data is new and half is old or zero.

In Wally: Detected by a zero length or a bad checksum, and cut off during crash recovery.

docs.title: VarHandle
docs.text:
In general: A Java tool for reading and writing a variable or memory location with special rules: atomically, or with acquire / release ordering.

In Wally: The Mem class wraps VarHandles to read and write ints and longs in MemorySegments with the right ordering.

docs.title: Write-Ahead Log (WAL)
docs.text:
In general: A log where changes are written before they're applied, so after a crash the system can replay the log and recover. Used by almost every database.

In Wally: One of Wally's two modes: the log plus a flush policy, crash recovery and checkpoints.

docs.title: Zero-allocation
docs.text:
In general: Code that creates no new objects while it runs, so it gives the garbage collector nothing to do.

In Wally: Once warmed up, appending and reading records allocates nothing. Proven by JMH, by a per-thread allocation counter, and by the Epsilon GC test.

docs.title: Zero-copy
docs.text:
In general: Moving data without copying it from one buffer to another.

In Wally: With tryClaim, you write your data directly into the log's memory instead of building it somewhere else and copying it in.

docs.title: Tools mentioned in the docs
docs.text: Tool What it is jcstress OpenJDK tool that runs tiny concurrent tests millions of times to find memory-ordering bugs. Lincheck Tool that checks whether a concurrent data structure behaves like a correct single-threaded one. jqwik Property-based testing: generates thousands of random test cases and checks a rule holds for all of them. HdrHistogram Records latency measurements accurately, including the rare slow ones. MkDocs Turns these Markdown files into this website.

docs.title: Guarantees
docs.text:
Draft

Finalized and verified in M3.

docs.title: Durability per flush policy
docs.text:
Policy Survives process crash Survives OS crash / power loss Cost none() Yes, once committed (page cache) No guarantee Lowest latency periodic(d) Yes Records at or below flushedPosition(); up to d of data may be lost Group commit sync() Yes Yes, once append returns One force() per append

macOS

msync/fsync on macOS does not guarantee data reaches stable storage. True durability needs F_FULLFSYNC. Treat macOS as a development platform.

docs.title: Visibility and ordering
docs.text:
• A record is visible to tailers once its length is published with release semantics.
  • Tailers see records in position order. They never skip an uncommitted record; they wait at it.
  • With multiple producers, position order is claim order, not commit order.

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text: On open, Wally scans from the last checkpoint and truncates at the first uncommitted or CRC-invalid record. Recovery never surfaces a corrupt record.

docs.title: How Wally works (and the Java behind it)
docs.text:
This page explains what Wally will do, follows one record from start to finish, then goes through each Java concept Wally relies on and shows where it appears in the real code.

If a word is unfamiliar, check the Glossary.

docs.title: What Wally will do
docs.text: Capability What it means for you Status Append records Write chunks of bytes to the end of the log, from one or many threads ✅ single segment, single writer (M0) Zero-copy writes Reserve space and write directly into the log ✅ (M0) Read records in order Get every record, in order, through a callback ✅ (M0) No GC pressure No objects created per record once warmed up ✅ proven (M0) Store in files Records live in memory-mapped segment files; the log grows across files M1 Checksums Detect corrupted records M1 Many producers Several threads append at once without locks M2 Durability control Choose how often data is forced to disk M3 Crash recovery Restart after a crash with a correct, uncorrupted log M3 Named consumers Readers that remember their place across restarts M4 Automatic cleanup Delete old files once everyone has read them M4

docs.title: The life of a record
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Producer thread
    participant L as Log memory (segment)
    participant C as Consumer thread
    P->>L: 1. Claim 40 bytes at the tail (length field still 0)
    P->>L: 2. Write header type + payload bytes
    C->>L: reads length = 0 → "not ready", waits
    P->>L: 3. Commit: write length = 40 (release)
    C->>L: reads length = 40 (acquire) → whole record is visible
    C->>C: 4. Calls your handler with (buffer, offset, length, position)
  1. Claim. The producer reserves space at the end of the log. Nobody else can get that space.
  2. Write. The producer fills in the record: either Wally copies your bytes in, or you write them yourself (zero-copy).
  3. Commit. The producer writes the record's length last. This single write is what makes the record "exist" for readers.
  4. Read. The consumer sees a non-zero length, reads the record, and moves on to the next one, which starts at the next multiple of 8 bytes.

Here is how a record is laid out in memory:

byte:  0         4        6        8         12        16
       ┌─────────┬────────┬────────┬─────────┬─────────┬───────────────┬───────┐
       │ length  │ type   │ flags  │ crc32c  │reserved │ payload       │ pad   │
       │ int     │ short  │ short  │ int     │ int     │ (your bytes)  │ 0–7 B │
       └─────────┴────────┴────────┴─────────┴─────────┴───────────────┴───────┘
       ◄──────────────── 16-byte header ──────────────►

docs.title: Java concepts, and how Wally uses them
1. The heap, objects and garbage collection
docs.text:
The concept. In Java, new Order() creates an object on the heap. You never free it yourself. When nothing refers to it anymore, the garbage collector (GC) reclaims the memory. That's convenient, but the GC has to find and clean up dead objects, and parts of that work can pause your program.

Why it matters for Wally. A typical queue creates at least one object per message. At 10 million messages per second, that's 10 million objects per second for the GC to deal with.

What Wally does. It keeps record data outside the heap and creates no objects per record. The benchmarks show the difference: ArrayBlockingQueue allocates 48 bytes per 32-byte message; Wally allocates about 0.

docs.title: 2. Off-heap memory: Arena and MemorySegment
docs.text:
The concept. Java's FFM API (final in Java 22) lets you work with raw memory safely:

  • An Arena owns some memory and decides when it's freed.
  • A MemorySegment is a handle to that memory. It knows its size, so reading past the end throws an exception instead of corrupting memory.
  • A ValueLayout (JAVA_INT, JAVA_LONG, JAVA_SHORT...) says how to read or write a value at an offset.
MemorySegment buffer = Arena.ofAuto().allocate(1 << 20, 4096);  // 1 MB, page-aligned, zero-filled
buffer.set(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, 16, 42L);                     // write a long at byte 16
long value = buffer.get(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, 16);             // read it back

In Wally. SegmentWriter and SegmentReader work entirely on a MemorySegment. For example, writing the record type in SegmentWriter.tryClaim:

buffer.set(ValueLayout.JAVA_SHORT, offset + TYPE_OFFSET, RecordFormat.TYPE_DATA);

Before the FFM API, libraries like this used sun.misc.Unsafe, an internal class that was never officially supported and is now being removed. See ADR 0001.

docs.title: 3. Memory-mapped files (coming in M1)
docs.text:
The concept. FileChannel.map(...) asks the operating system to make a file appear as memory. Writing to the returned MemorySegment writes to the file. The OS moves data to disk in the background, and segment.force() makes it happen right now.

try (FileChannel channel = FileChannel.open(path, READ, WRITE, CREATE)) {
    MemorySegment file = channel.map(FileChannel.MapMode.READ_WRITE, 0, size, arena);
    // file is now a MemorySegment backed by the file on disk
}

In Wally. The same SegmentWriter and SegmentReader code works unchanged on a mapped file, because both are just MemorySegments. Closing the arena unmaps the file immediately. The older MappedByteBuffer API had no way to do that.

docs.title: 4. Threads and the Java Memory Model
docs.text:
The concept. A thread is an independent path of execution. Threads share memory, which creates a surprising problem: to go faster, the CPU and the compiler may reorder memory writes. If thread A writes the payload and then the length, thread B might see the new length before the payload.

The Java Memory Model defines when one thread is guaranteed to see another's writes. The key idea is happens-before: if thread A does a release write and thread B sees it with an acquire read, everything A wrote before the release is visible to B.

In Wally. This is exactly the "write the record, then sign it" rule. Commit is a release write of the length (RecordFormat.publish):

public static void publish(MemorySegment buffer, long frameOffset, int frameLength) {
    Mem.setIntRelease(buffer, frameOffset + FRAME_LENGTH_OFFSET, frameLength);
}

And the reader starts every record with an acquire read (SegmentReader.read):

int frameLength = Mem.getIntAcquire(buffer, offset);
if (frameLength == 0) {
    break;   // not committed yet: stop here and try again later
}

The test readerOnOtherThreadSeesEveryRecordInOrder writes 1 million records on one thread and checks that another thread reads every one, in order.

docs.title: 5. VarHandle: ordered and atomic memory access
docs.text:
The concept. A VarHandle is Java's tool for reading and writing memory with special rules: plain, acquire, release, volatile, or atomic operations like getAndAdd and compareAndSet. The FFM API can give you a VarHandle for any ValueLayout.

In Wally. The Mem class keeps one VarHandle per type and wraps it in clearly named methods:

private static final VarHandle INT = ValueLayout.JAVA_INT.varHandle();

public static int getIntAcquire(MemorySegment segment, long offset) {
    return (int) INT.getAcquire(segment, offset);
}

public static long getAndAddLong(MemorySegment segment, long offset, long delta) {
    return (long) LONG.getAndAdd(segment, offset, delta);
}

getAndAddLong will hand out space to multiple producers in M2. It's the "deli counter ticket" from the home page: each producer adds its record size to the tail and gets back where its own slot starts, in a single CPU instruction, with no lock.

Why (int) casts?

VarHandle methods are signature polymorphic: the JVM uses the exact argument and return types you write to pick a fast path. The cast tells it the return type, and static final lets the JIT compiler turn the call into a single machine instruction.

docs.title: 6. Interfaces and lambdas, without allocation
docs.text:
The concept. An interface declares methods without implementing them. A functional interface has exactly one method, so you can pass a lambda (a short inline function) wherever one is expected.

In Wally. Reading uses a callback, so Wally never has to create an object per record to hand it to you:

@FunctionalInterface
public interface RecordHandler {
    void onRecord(MemorySegment buffer, long offset, int length, long position);
}

reader.read((buffer, offset, length, position) -> {
    long orderId = buffer.get(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, offset);
    // ...
}, 100);

Lambdas can allocate

A lambda that uses local variables from around it (a capturing lambda) may create a new object every time that line runs. To stay zero-allocation, create your handler once and reuse it, or make your class implement RecordHandler, as the test helper AllocationLoop does.

docs.title: 7. The flyweight pattern: reusing one object
docs.text:
The concept. Instead of creating an object for every piece of data, keep one object and point it at different data each time.

In Wally. SegmentWriter itself implements the Claim interface. After tryClaim, the same writer object describes the claimed space:

long position = writer.tryClaim(8);
writer.buffer().set(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, writer.offset(), 42L);  // write directly into the log
writer.commit();

One object serves every record, so there is nothing for the GC to collect.

docs.title: 8. Return codes instead of exceptions on the hot path
docs.text:
The concept. Java exceptions are great for real errors, but creating one captures a stack trace, which allocates memory and is slow.

In Wally. An expected situation, like "the segment is full", is reported with a return value:

if (writer.append(src, 0, 64) == SegmentWriter.NO_SPACE) {
    // move to the next segment (M1 does this for you)
}

Programming mistakes, like a negative length or committing twice, still throw exceptions, because they should never happen in correct code.

docs.title: 9. try / finally for consistent state
docs.text:
The concept. A finally block always runs, even if an exception is thrown.

In Wally. If your handler throws, the reader still saves how far it got, so the failing record isn't delivered again in an endless loop:

try {
    while (count < recordLimit && offset < limit) { /* deliver records */ }
} finally {
    this.offset = offset;
}

docs.title: 10. Java modules (module-info.java)
docs.text:
The concept. A module declares which packages other code may use.

In Wally.

module io.wally.core {
    exports io.wally.api;
}

Only io.wally.api is visible to users. Everything under io.wally.internal can change freely without breaking anyone.

docs.title: 11. Proving it: measuring allocation
docs.text:
How do we know Wally doesn't allocate? Three independent checks:

Check How it works Where Per-thread counter ThreadMXBean.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() before and after 1M records; must be under 1 KB ZeroAllocationTest Epsilon GC Runs 50M records with a GC that never frees memory and a 128 MB heap. Any per-record allocation would run out of memory ./gradlew :wally-core:epsilonTest JMH profiler Reports bytes allocated per operation: ≈ 0.0001 ./gradlew :wally-bench:jmh -Pjmh.profilers=gc

docs.title: Code map
docs.text: File Role api/RecordHandler.java Callback you implement to receive records api/Claim.java Reserved space you write into, then commit or abort internal/memory/Mem.java Acquire/release and atomic reads/writes on off-heap memory internal/memory/Align.java Rounding up to multiples of 8 internal/log/RecordFormat.java Record header layout, publish and padding helpers internal/log/SegmentWriter.java Appends records to one segment; doubles as the Claim internal/log/SegmentReader.java Reads committed records from one segment

docs.title: Record layout
docs.text: Every record starts at an offset that is a multiple of 8 bytes. After a record ends, 0–7 padding bytes are added so the next record starts at the next 8-byte boundary.

docs.title: Header: 16 bytes
docs.text: Byte offset Size (bytes) Java type Field name Purpose 0 4 int frameLength Total frame size: header (16) + payload bytes. 0 means "not committed yet". Written last with release semantics. 4 2 short type 1 = DATA (your record), 2 = PADDING (fills gaps) 6 2 short flags Reserved for future use (currently unused) 8 4 int crc32c CRC32C checksum of the payload. 0 when checksums are disabled. 12 4 int reserved Reserved (currently unused)

docs.title: Payload: variable length
docs.text: Byte offset Size (bytes) Contents 16 frameLength - 16 Your data (the bytes you appended)

docs.title: Alignment padding: 0–7 bytes
docs.text:
After the payload ends, the next record must start at a multiple of 8. So if your payload is 19 bytes:

  • Header: 16 bytes
  • Payload: 19 bytes
  • Total so far: 35 bytes
  • Next multiple of 8: 40 bytes
  • Padding added: 5 bytes

The padding bytes are not part of the record. They are just wasted space to keep the next record aligned.

docs.title: Example 2: 64-byte payload (already aligned)
docs.text:
Byte:  0    ...    15   16   ...   79   80
      ┌───────────────┬──────────────┬────┐
Field │ 16 B header   │ 64 B payload │next│
      │frameLength=80 │              │rec │
      └───────────────┴──────────────┴────┘
  • frameLength = 16 + 64 = 80 bytes
  • 80 is already a multiple of 8, so no padding
  • Next record starts at byte 80

docs.title: Example 3: PADDING frame (fills end of segment)
docs.text:
When a record doesn't fit in the remaining space, a PADDING frame is written:

Byte:  0    1    2    3    4    5    6    7
      ┌────┬────┬────┬────┬────┬────┬────┬────┐
      │frameLength=1000   │type│    │ (unused)  │
      │                   │ =2 │    │           │
      └────┴────┴────┴────┴────┴────┴────┴────┘
  • frameLength = however many bytes remain (could be 8, could be 1000)
  • type = 2 (PADDING)
  • Everything else is ignored
  • Readers skip padding frames and move to the next segment

docs.title: Why frameLength includes the header
docs.text:
If frameLength held only the payload length:

  • A padding frame with no payload would be frameLength = 0
  • But 0 already means "not committed"

So frameLength = header + payload. A minimum-size padding frame is 8 bytes: frameLength = 8, type = 2, and that's it. The reader knows to skip the next 8 bytes and keep going.

docs.title: In the code
docs.text:
The layout is defined in io.wally.internal.log.RecordFormat:

public static final int ALIGNMENT = 8;
public static final int HEADER_LENGTH = 16;

public static final int FRAME_LENGTH_OFFSET = 0;
public static final int TYPE_OFFSET = 4;
public static final int FLAGS_OFFSET = 6;
public static final int CRC_OFFSET = 8;

public static final short TYPE_DATA = 1;
public static final short TYPE_PADDING = 2;

Commit uses a release write:

public static void publish(MemorySegment buffer, long frameOffset, int frameLength) {
    Mem.setIntRelease(buffer, frameOffset + FRAME_LENGTH_OFFSET, frameLength);
}

And the reader uses an acquire read:

int frameLength = Mem.getIntAcquire(buffer, offset);
if (frameLength == 0) {
    break;   // not committed yet
}

See How Wally works for why this guarantees that once the reader sees the length, it sees the complete record.

docs.title: Roadmap: MVP (M0–M4)
docs.text:
Target: JDK 25 LTS (final FFM API), Gradle Kotlin DSL, zero runtime dependencies in wally-core.

flowchart LR
  M0[M0 memory layer] --> M1[M1 mmap segments] --> M2[M2 MPSC] --> M3[M3 durability + recovery] --> M4[M4 consumer groups + retention]

docs.title: M0: memory layer + in-memory log ✅
docs.text:
• Mem (static aligned VarHandles: acquire/release, volatile, getAndAdd, CAS) and Align.
  • RecordFormat: int frameLength | short type | short flags | int crc | int reserved (16 B header, 8 B alignment). frameLength == 0 means uncommitted. TYPE_PADDING fills the end of a segment and replaces aborted claims.
  • SegmentWriter (single writer; doubles as the Claim flyweight) and SegmentReader over one off-heap segment.
  • Read API: RecordHandler.onRecord(MemorySegment seg, long offset, int length, long position), so there are no slices.
  • JMH single-thread append + read vs ArrayBlockingQueue (payloads 32 B, 256 B, 4 KB). Cross-thread benchmarks moved to M2, since a single fixed segment can't sustain a long 1P1C run.

Exit (met): unit tests pass, including a cross-thread ordering test; JMH -prof gc shows gc.alloc.rate.norm ≈ 10⁻⁴ B/op; ThreadMXBean check shows < 1 KB over 1M records; Epsilon GC test passes (-Xmx128m, 50M records).

docs.title: M1: mmap'd segments, single writer
docs.text:
• 64 B segment header: magic WALLY\0, format version, segment size, base position, header CRC.
  • SegmentFile maps with FileChannel.map(READ_WRITE, 0, size, arena). Unmap is arena.close(), gated by a refcount.
  • Position = segmentIndex * segmentSize + offset (ADR 0002).
  • Rollover writes PADDING, then maps the next segment. A Preallocator agent creates and pre-touches segment N+1.
  • Appender.append(...) and tryClaim(len) → reused Claim flyweight (segment(), offset(), commit(), abort()).
  • ChecksumMode {NONE, CRC32C}. Risk: java.util.zip.CRC32C over asByteBuffer() may allocate; fall back to a slice-by-8 implementation reading from the MemorySegment.

Exit: jqwik model test (random append/poll/reopen/segment sizes vs ArrayList oracle) passes; rollover tested at exact boundaries; File format written.

docs.title: M2: multi-producer claim/commit
docs.text:
• PaddedCounter (value isolated by 128 B padding) for the shared tail.
  • Tail claim with getAndAdd (ADR 0004). The claimant whose range covers the end of a segment writes padding and triggers the roll; claimants landing past the end retry.
  • Commit: payload first, then setRelease(length). Reader: getAcquire(length) (ADR 0003).
  • producerMode(SINGLE | MULTI). Single mode uses a plain store.
  • jcstress (commit visibility, no torn header/payload) and Lincheck (MPSC append + tailer).
  • JMH NP1C (N = 1, 2, 4, 8) with HdrHistogram and a fixed-rate driver.

Exit: no forbidden jcstress outcomes; Lincheck passes; still zero allocation.

docs.title: M3: durability + crash recovery
docs.text:
• FlushPolicy.none() | periodic(Duration) | sync(). Periodic = flusher agent force()s dirty ranges (group commit).
  • Appender.flushedPosition() exposes the durable watermark.
  • Recovery on open: validate headers → scan from checkpoint → stop at first zero length / bad CRC → zero the tail.
  • Crash harness: child JVM appends with sync() and reports acked positions; parent kill -9s it at random times, reopens, and asserts the prefix property.
  • Corruption tests: random byte flips and truncation.

Exit: 1,000 crash iterations green locally and in Linux CI; Guarantees written.

docs.title: M4: consumer groups + retention
docs.text:
• CursorFile: small mmap'd file with fixed slots (name hash + 64 B name + padded position).
  • wal.tailer("group") resumes from the persisted cursor; commit(), seek(position). Ad-hoc wal.tailerFrom(position) is not persisted.
  • Retention agent deletes segments wholly below min(group cursors, checkpoint) after the refcount drains.
  • RetentionPolicy.wal() (truncate on checkpoint(position)) vs RetentionPolicy.queue(maxSegments) (appender returns BACK_PRESSURED).
  • WaitStrategy: busy-spin / yield / park.
  • Examples: event-sourcing journal, inter-thread pipeline.

Exit: model test extended with groups, restart and retention; 30-minute soak shows no fd or mapping leaks; Concepts and quickstart docs complete.

docs.title: Out of scope for MVP
docs.text: CLI tools, SBE codec, Micrometer metrics, cross-process IPC, stuck-producer unblocker, LazyFS power-loss tests, Jazzer fuzzing, Maven Central publishing.

docs.title: Verification commands
docs.text: Command Checks ./gradlew build Unit, jqwik and Lincheck tests ./gradlew :wally-stress:jcstress Memory ordering ./gradlew :wally-core:crashTest kill -9 recovery harness ./gradlew :wally-bench:jmh -Pjmh.profilers=gc gc.alloc.rate.norm ≈ 0 ./gradlew :wally-core:epsilonTest Zero allocation under Epsilon GC mkdocs serve Docs render locally

docs.title: ADR 0001: Use the FFM API instead of Unsafe
docs.text: Status: Accepted · Date: 2026-11-05

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Wally needs off-heap memory, memory-mapped files, atomic operations on raw memory, and deterministic unmapping. Historically this meant sun.misc.Unsafe + MappedByteBuffer.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Target JDK 25 LTS and use the final Foreign Function & Memory API: MemorySegment, Arena, ValueLayout.varHandle() for atomics, FileChannel.map(..., arena) for mapping, and Linker for madvise.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• + Supported API: Unsafe memory access warns from JDK 24 and is slated for removal.
  • + arena.close() unmaps deterministically. No more relying on GC to unmap.
  • + Bounds and liveness checks, which the JIT removes on hot paths.
  • − Requires JDK 22+ (we pick 25 LTS). Excludes users stuck on 17/21.
  • − asSlice() allocates, so the API exposes (segment, offset, length) triples.
  • − Closing a shared arena while another thread is using it throws, so segment lifetime needs refcounting.

docs.title: ADR 0002: Address records by logical byte position
docs.text: Status: Accepted · Date: 2026-11-05

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Consumers and checkpoints need a stable, seekable identifier for a record. Options: a sequence number (needs an index file) or a byte position.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Identify records by a 64-bit logical position = segmentIndex * segmentSize + offsetInSegment. segmentSize is a power of two and fixed per log.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• + O(1) seek: segmentIndex = pos >>> log2(segmentSize), offset = pos & (segmentSize - 1). No index file.
  • + The tail counter, cursors and checkpoints are all plain longs, so they are cheap to CAS and persist.
  • − Positions are not dense: users can't compute "the Nth record". A sparse sequence index can come later if needed.
  • − Segment size can't change for an existing log.

docs.title: ADR 0003: Two-phase claim/commit with length as the commit marker
docs.text: Status: Accepted · Date: 2026-11-05

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Producers must write records in place (zero copy) while readers scan concurrently, without locks. Readers must never observe a partially written record.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Claim: reserve align8(16 + len) bytes at the tail. The frameLength field is still 0.
  2. Write: fill type, flags, CRC and payload with plain stores.
  3. Commit: store frameLength (header + payload) with setRelease.

Readers load frameLength with getAcquire. 0 means "not committed", so stop. A positive value guarantees the rest of the record is visible (release/acquire happens-before).

Segments are zero-filled on creation, so unwritten space always reads as frameLength == 0. Aborted claims are rewritten as padding frames.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• + One release store per record; no locks, no CAS on the read path.
  • + Torn writes after a crash show up as frameLength == 0 or a CRC mismatch, which makes recovery simple.
  • − A producer that dies between claim and commit leaves a hole that blocks readers. Mitigation (post-MVP): an unblocker that pads over holes after a timeout.
  • − Max payload is bounded by int and by segment size minus headers.

docs.title: ADR 0004: Claim tail space with fetch-add, not a CAS loop
docs.text: Status: Accepted · Date: 2026-11-05

docs.title: Context
docs.text: In multi-producer mode, producers contend on the tail counter. A CAS loop retries under contention; fetch-add (LOCK XADD on x86, LDADD on ARMv8.1+) always succeeds in one instruction.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Producers claim with getAndAdd(tail, recordLength). If the returned range crosses the segment end:

  • The claimant whose range covers the segment end writes a PADDING record from its start to the end, then triggers the roll.
  • Claimants whose range starts at or past the end don't write anything. They wait for the next segment to become active and retry there.

Single-producer mode skips the atomic and uses a plain store plus release.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• + Wait-free claim in the common case; throughput scales better than a CAS loop under contention.
  • − The tail can overshoot the segment end, so the logical tail must be re-based on roll. This needs careful jcstress coverage.
  • − Overshooting claimants waste a small amount of address space (no disk space).

docs.title: 0. Core idea
docs.text:
Build one thing: an append-only log addressed by position. Both modes sit on top of it:

  • WAL = log + durability policy + crash recovery + truncation at checkpoints.
  • Event queue = log + named consumer cursors + retention (delete a segment once every cursor has passed it).

Prior art worth studying: Agrona and Aeron (log buffers), Chronicle Queue, the LMAX Disruptor.

Foundational decision: use the Java 22+ FFM API (MemorySegment, Arena, VarHandle) instead of sun.misc.Unsafe. See ADR 0001.

  • JDK 24+ warns on Unsafe memory access, and it is headed for removal.
  • FileChannel.map(mode, off, size, arena) gives deterministic unmapping with arena.close(). That fixes the old MappedByteBuffer unmap problem.
  • Linker allows calling madvise/mlock without JNI.

docs.title: 1. Problems to solve
docs.text:
# Problem Approach 1 Record framing 8-byte aligned header: int length, short type, short flags, int crc32c, then the payload. Little-endian, fixed. A PADDING record type fills the rest of a segment. 2 Atomic publish Two-phase claim/commit. A producer reserves space, writes the payload, then writes length last with setRelease. Readers getAcquire the length; 0 means "not committed yet, stop here." 3 Multi-producer contention getAndAdd on the tail counter (fetch-add, not a CAS loop, so there are no retries). 128-byte padding around hot counters to avoid false sharing. Single-writer first, then MPSC. 4 Segment rollover Fixed-size segment files (e.g. 1 GiB). The producer whose claim crosses the boundary writes the padding and triggers the roll; other producers retry. Logical position is segmentIdx * segSize + offset, so seeking is O(1) with no index file. 5 Page-fault stalls A background thread pre-allocates and pre-touches the next segment, plus madvise(SEQUENTIAL/WILLNEED). Document THP and vm.dirty_* tuning. 6 Durability mmap writes only reach the page cache. Flush policies NONE, PERIODIC (group commit every N ms) and SYNC, via MemorySegment.force(). macOS needs F_FULLFSYNC for real durability. Document what "acknowledged" means for each policy. 7 Crash recovery On open, scan forward from the last checkpoint and validate each CRC. Truncate at the first torn or zero frame. File header: magic + format version + segment size. 8 Stuck producer (hole) A producer thread that dies between claim and commit blocks readers forever. Fix (post-MVP): after a timeout, an "unblocker" writes padding over the hole (as Aeron does). 9 Segment lifetime vs. readers Closing a shared Arena while a reader is using it throws. Reference counting or epoch-based reclamation before unmapping or deleting. 10 Zero allocation MemorySegment.asSlice() allocates. Expose (segment, offset, length) instead of slices. Reused flyweights, non-capturing or pre-allocated handlers, return codes instead of exceptions. No iterators, boxing or varargs on the hot path. 11 Backpressure / waiting WaitStrategy: busy-spin, then Thread.onSpinWait, then yield, then park. Queue mode returns BACK_PRESSURED when retention would be exceeded. 12 Cross-process (post-MVP) Shared mmap'd metadata file holding the tail and cursors. Aligned CAS on mapped memory works across processes.

State the claims precisely

  • "Zero-allocation" means steady state on the hot path.
  • "Lock-free" means the append and read paths; fsync is not lock-free.

docs.title: 2. Code organization
docs.text:
Gradle multi-module build. Core has no runtime dependencies. JPMS module-info exports only io.wally.api.

wally/
├─ wally-core/        # io.wally.api              public: Wally, Appender, Claim, Tailer, configs
│                     # io.wally.internal.memory  FFM, VarHandles, alignment, native madvise
│                     # io.wally.internal.log     framing, appender, reader
│                     # io.wally.internal.segment mapping, rolling, preallocation, refcount
│                     # io.wally.internal.recovery scan, CRC verify, truncate
│                     # io.wally.internal.concurrent padded counters, wait strategies, agents
│                     # io.wally.internal.queue   consumer groups, cursors, retention
├─ wally-bench/       # JMH
├─ wally-stress/      # jcstress + Lincheck
├─ wally-examples/    # event-sourcing journal, inter-thread pipeline
├─ docs/              # this site + ADRs
│  (post-MVP)
├─ wally-codec-sbe/   # optional SBE integration
├─ wally-metrics/     # optional Micrometer binding
└─ wally-tools/       # CLI: dump / verify / recover / stats

docs.title: API shape (sketch)
docs.text:
try (Wally wal = Wally.builder().dir(p).segmentSize(1 << 30)
        .flush(FlushPolicy.periodic(Duration.ofMillis(5))).open()) {
    Appender a = wal.appender();                  // one per thread, reused
    long pos = a.append(src, off, len);           // copy path
    Claim c = a.tryClaim(64);                     // zero-copy path, reused flyweight
    if (c != null) { c.segment().set(JAVA_LONG, c.offset(), 42L); c.commit(); }

    Tailer t = wal.tailer("billing");             // named, persisted cursor
    t.poll((seg, off, len, position) -> { ... }, 256);
}

Methods return long positions, with negative constants for BACK_PRESSURED, ROLLING and CLOSED (the Aeron style).

docs.title: 3. Patterns
docs.text:
• Flyweight: Claim and record views over raw memory, with no per-message objects.
  • Two-phase claim/commit: the publish protocol.
  • Single Writer Principle: the default mode. MPSC is opt-in.
  • Sequence/cursor (Disruptor): consumers are just positions.
  • Strategy: WaitStrategy, FlushPolicy, RetentionPolicy.
  • Builder + immutable config.
  • Agent / duty cycle (Agrona): background flusher, preallocator and retention cleaner on one optional thread.
  • ADRs: every non-obvious decision is recorded in docs/adr/.

docs.title: 4. Utility
docs.text:
• Target use cases, each shipped as an example: event-sourcing journal, local durable outbox in front of Kafka, inter-thread pipeline, replication log for a KV store.
  • Zero dependencies in core, published to Maven Central.
  • Explicit guarantees table: what survives a process crash vs. a power loss under each FlushPolicy. See Guarantees.
  • CLI tooling to inspect and repair files.
  • Stability: file-format versioning, API compatibility checks with japicmp, semver.
  • Honest benchmarks against ArrayBlockingQueue, JCTools MPSC, Disruptor and Chronicle Queue, with reproducible scripts.

docs.text: Layer Tool What it covers Unit JUnit 5 Framing, alignment, padding, rollover at exact boundaries, CRC Model-based jqwik Random append/poll/roll/reopen sequences checked against an ArrayList oracle Memory ordering jcstress Claim → commit → read visibility; no torn length/payload observed Linearizability Lincheck MPSC append + concurrent tailers Crash Child JVM + kill -9 mid-write, then reopen Prefix property: every durable-acknowledged record is present and no corrupt record is surfaced Power loss LazyFS (FUSE that drops unsynced writes), Linux CI Validates FlushPolicy guarantees for real Corruption Jazzer fuzzing of the recovery scanner; random byte flips and truncation Recovery never crashes or returns garbage Soak Multi-hour run with rollover + retention Leaks, file-descriptor growth, mapping leaks

docs.title: Non-functional
docs.text:
• Throughput and latency: JMH across 1P1C and NP1C, payloads from 32 B to 4 KB. HdrHistogram with a fixed-rate load generator so coordinated omission doesn't hide tail latency. Report p50/p99/p99.99/max.
  • Zero-allocation proof:
    • JMH -prof gc: assert gc.alloc.rate.norm == 0.
    • Steady-state run under -XX:+UseEpsilonGC with a small heap. Any allocation eventually exhausts the heap and fails the run.
    • JFR allocation events as a cross-check.
  • Profiling: async-profiler and JMH -prof perfasm.
  • Durability cost: throughput vs. flush interval curve.
  • Environment: real numbers on dedicated Linux with pinned cores and isolcpus. CI perf checks only as coarse regression gates.
  • Matrix: JDK 25 LTS × Linux x86/ARM × macOS.
